episodes.title: Lynching of John and Edward Lovelace
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.doubt: single wire story (Advocate dateline Aug 10; 'Monday'); accusation reversed: the Lovelaces had accused Oscar Parks of stealing their corn and were killed for refusing to retract
episodes.summary: The lynching of John and Edward Lovelace was the shooting of a Black farmer and his son by a group of white men at their home in Woodbury, Georgia, in August 1910. According to the wire report, the men were killed to punish them for saying that a white man had stolen their corn. The dispatch ran in white papers from Mississippi and Louisiana to Ohio and Washington and in the Black weekly the Advocate, which headlined the white men as the accused robbers.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jack Nelson
episodes.doubt: name Jack Nelson only in one distant paper (Cairo, Ill. dateline); Saturday July 30 vs Sunday July 31; no county named
episodes.summary: The lynching of Jack Nelson was the hanging and shooting of a Black man by a gathering of neighbors near Cairo, Georgia, on the night of July 30, 1910. He was accused of entering the bedroom of the young daughter of a farmer, John Wade, and was dragged from under her bed, hanged from a tree limb and shot. The story ran across the country on the wires, often under a mistaken Cairo, Illinois, dateline, and reached two Black weeklies only as a single sentence in a syndicated news column.

episodes.title: Bill Walker manhunt and false lynching report
episodes.doubt: B-T bt:4744 lists a lynching; the press shows the lynching wire was false: a posse and a train fireman fired on Walker at Cold Creek, he was jailed, tried and convicted (Neal 2026-11-13: keep link, don't count)
episodes.summary: The Bill Walker manhunt was the pursuit of Bill Walker, a Black man, by sheriff's posses in Mobile County, Alabama, beginning July 31, 1910, after he was accused of assaulting a white woman at Axis and killing a Black man. Wire services reported on August 1 that a mob had shot him to death and burned his body. Mobile dispatches showed instead that he escaped posse gunfire, was arrested in Mississippi, guarded in jail against lynching, and convicted of murder on September 8.

episodes.title: Killing of William Beardsley
episodes.summary: The killing of William Beardsley took place on August 7, 1910, when Deputy Sheriff William Nugent shot and killed Beardsley, a Black man, in a freight car in the N. O., M. and C. Railroad yards at Mobile, Alabama. Nugent and a second deputy had come to arrest him on an assault charge, and the only reports found, all in the Montgomery Advertiser, described the shooting as self-defense. Bessie Cannon, a Black woman who was in the car, was afterward held for the grand jury on a charge of assault to murder.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jim Toler
episodes.summary: The lynching of Jim Toler was the killing of a Black man by a mob of more than 100 men at Alamo, near Helena in Montgomery County, Georgia, early on the morning of August 11, 1910. Toler was accused of entering the bedroom of two daughters of a planter while they slept; a posse found him in a field the next day, and he was tied to a tree and shot to death. A single dispatch from Helena carried the story to papers from Maine to New Mexico over the following week, while no Georgia or Black newspaper account and no report of an inquest or arrest was found.

episodes.title: Durham Brothers turpentine still whitecapping case
episodes.summary: The Durham Brothers turpentine still whitecapping case was the arrest in late August 1910 of two white men, William McLemore and Frank Parker, accused of driving a Black worker away at gunpoint from a turpentine still about eight miles south of Poplarville, Mississippi. The Hattiesburg News, the only paper found to report the case, presented the arrests as a hoped-for end to months of terror among the still's Black workers and to a labor shortage costly to the turpentine business.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Thomas Wayne
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Thomas Wayne took place at Hinton, West Virginia, on August 16, 1910, when a crowd of 1,000 or more tried to seize a Black prisoner charged with assaulting and killing Mrs. John Alliff near Quinnimont. The sheriff slipped away with him after dark while the governor sent militia, and the Advocate of Charleston, a Black weekly, condemned the mob's reported cry that he was "only a nigger."

episodes.title: Pelham gambling-house raid shooting
episodes.summary: The Pelham gambling-house raid shooting took place on August 1, 1910, when a sheriff's posse and Pelham officers fired into a house near Pelham, Georgia, where a group of Black men were said to be gambling. Between one and three of the men were reported killed and several more wounded, and no white man was hurt. Two wire versions with different death tolls ran in papers from Alabama to New York, and a Georgia follow-up described fears of a 'general riot' in the town.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of James Bradford
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of James Bradford took place on the night of August 6, 1910, when a crowd gathered outside the Culver building in downtown St. Louis, Missouri, shouting for the lynching of Bradford, a Black janitor whom police had just arrested on the accusation of luring a young white woman, Bessie Unger, to his room with a false job advertisement. Police removed Bradford from the crowd, and he was later bound over to a grand jury on two charges. Dispatches about the case ran in white papers across the country, several under headlines that linked it to lynching.

episodes.title: Mob attack on the Looker building, Moline, Illinois
episodes.summary: The mob attack on the Looker building took place in Moline, Illinois, on the night of 15 August 1910, when about 50 white men, many armed, surrounded a building said to house about 100 Black residents and smashed its windows with rocks. The crowd had gathered after a report that two Black men had pursued a white girl, and three police officers dispersed it before anyone was reported hurt. The Rock Island Argus presented the night as a narrowly averted "race clash," and a wire item carried a larger version of it as far as Spokane.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Tom Hayes
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Tom Hayes was a failed attempt by a mob to take Tom Hayes (also spelled Hays), a Black man accused of murder, from the jail at Andalusia, Covington County, Alabama, on the night of August 24–25, 1910. According to Sheriff W. T. Prestwood, a mob gathered a few miles from town, but its advance party turned back after finding the jail guarded by the local militia company. Hayes was taken the next morning to the Montgomery County jail, where he had been held after a crowd pursued him at his arrest in July. The Montgomery Advertiser, the Birmingham Age-Herald and the Pensacola Journal each reported the episode as a narrow escape from lynching.

episodes.title: Lynchings at Dady, Florida
episodes.doubt: most reports two men hanged July 30 (1-6 in others); B-T and MWT list three; the Aug 1 'fourth' killing denied locally
episodes.summary: The lynchings at Dady, Florida, took place on July 30, 1910, when a mob of white men took two Black men accused of murdering a white schoolgirl from the Holmes County sheriff and hanged and shot them on a road between Dady and Bonifay. Later dispatches reported a manhunt and further killings, putting the toll anywhere from one to six; the Pensacola Journal said a reported fourth killing had not happened. Some Black newspapers carried the story as short wire items.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Dick Lee
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Dick Lee took place at Stanford, Kentucky, in late August 1910, when friends of two white men Lee was accused of stabbing at Moreland talked of storming the jail at Stanford to lynch him. No attempt was made, and Lee was held in jail for the grand jury.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Will Ingram
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Will Ingram took place in Eatonton, Putnam County, Georgia, on July 30 or 31, 1910, when a crowd pursued and fired at Ingram, a Black man accused of burglary, after he escaped from custody. Ingram survived after a white woman, Mrs. Susie Hillhouse, stood between him and the crowd, and he was returned to jail. Dispatches built around her intervention ran in papers from New York to Washington State and on the front page of the Black newspaper The Advocate.

episodes.title: Killing of Charles Davis
episodes.summary: The killing of Charles Davis took place near Denmark, South Carolina, on August 27, 1910, when Davis, a Black man wanted for the killing of Lucy Dwight, was shot as he fled an arranged arrest by Magistrate S. G. Ray. He died of his wounds the next morning, and a coroner's jury in Orangeburg heard uncertain testimony on whether the dead man was in fact Davis. Local white papers in Orangeburg and Bamberg welcomed the shooting and praised the magistrate.

episodes.title: Shooting of Sam H. Hill
episodes.doubt: death only in the AP brief; the local dispatch has Hill alive Aug 20, 'probably fatally wounded'
episodes.summary: The shooting of Sam H. Hill took place near Arkansas City, Desha County, Arkansas, on August 19, 1910, when Deputy Sheriff J. P. Findley shot Hill, a Black man, after mistaking him for Henry Tucker, a fugitive wanted for the assault and murder of a white girl. The Associated Press reported Hill killed instantly, while a local dispatch described him as probably fatally wounded but still alive the next morning.

episodes.title: Killing of Relford Pollard
episodes.summary: The killing of Relford Pollard was the fatal shooting of a 34-year-old Black man by Richmond, Virginia, policeman W. J. Perkinson in a back yard on St. Peter Street on the evening of August 27, 1910. More than a thousand Black residents gathered after the shooting and were dispersed by police squads carrying riot guns. A coroner's jury and the Police Court exonerated Perkinson two days later, and the Richmond Planet denounced the shooting as an "unwarranted killing" and "useless slaughter."

episodes.title: Lynching of Nick Thompson
episodes.doubt: Aug 29 threats against an unnamed suspect, released Aug 30; Nick Thompson's lynching Sept 1 (bt:4750, MWT:2870) belongs to the September run
episodes.summary: The lynching of Nick Thompson took place near Amory, Mississippi, on September 1, 1910, when a mob reported at about 2,000 hanged Thompson, a Black man accused of assaulting a 17-year-old white girl, to a telegraph pole. Three days earlier, crowds had threatened to storm the jail to lynch another suspect, who was released as not the man sought. Wire reports stressing the crowd's size ran nationally, and a local weekly used the case to campaign for Vardaman.

episodes.title: Bradford police shooting of Wills Abbott
episodes.doubt: reported mortally wounded; no report of his death found
episodes.summary: The Bradford police shooting of Wills Abbott was a gun fight in early August 1910 at Bradford, Ohio, in which police officers mortally wounded Abbott, one of a group of Black men whose camp the officers had gone to investigate. Abbott's companions surrendered and were jailed. White newspapers from Illinois to Montana carried the story as a 'pitched battle' between police and 'a band of negroes', drawing on the officers' account; no Black-press coverage was found.

episodes.title: Killing of Tom Weaver
episodes.doubt: B-T bt:4747 lists a lynching; the press shows a posse with the mayor killing Weaver in an exchange of shots after he fired at the mayor (standard definition excludes an armed fugitive shot in pursuit); dossier to settle
episodes.summary: The killing of Tom Weaver was the fatal shooting of Tom Weaver, a Black man, by a posse of citizens at or near Seville, Georgia, on August 22, 1910. Weaver was accused of having fired a shotgun at Mayor Wilson, and the reports differ on whether he was shot down in the town's streets or killed in an exchange of fire at a house a few miles away. A brief wire dispatch carried the story to papers in New York, New Jersey, Connecticut and Wisconsin, while the Americus Times-Recorder printed a fuller report under a headline saying he had been "hanged by posse."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching at Dover, Delaware (1910)
episodes.doubt: local follow-ups reverse Turner's role: he was the man shot; Lewis W. Davis held
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching at Dover, Delaware, took place on the night of July 30 or 31, 1910, when a street crowd that included white men threatened to lynch Joseph "Tough" Turner, a Black man, after a shooting among Black men on Loockerman Street, the capital's busiest thoroughfare. Two policemen got the man away from the crowd, and no lynching took place. Wire reports named Turner as the gunman, but local follow-ups described him as the man who had been shot, and another Black man, Lewis W. Davis, was held on the charge.

episodes.title: Ordering out of Black visitors from Beatrice, Nebraska
episodes.summary: In August 1910 the police of Beatrice, Nebraska, ordered eight Black people out of the city after arresting four of them on vagrancy and vice charges. The eight left by train for Lincoln, and the authorities said they would keep similar newcomers out. The Beatrice Daily Express reported it under the headline "Population Decreasing," and a state-news column carried it elsewhere in Nebraska.

episodes.title: Buckner mob hunt, 1910
episodes.doubt: the girl said she did not see her attacker; the men questioned were released
episodes.summary: The Buckner mob hunt was an armed search for a Black man near Buckner, Missouri, on August 5, 1910, after Clara Baldus, a white farmer's daughter, was attacked in her home east of Independence. Wire reports said the mob threatened to burn the man if caught, but no report of a capture appears in the coverage. Fuller dispatches from Independence said the girl never saw her attacker, and the Black men questioned were released for lack of evidence.

episodes.title: Washington Circle pursuit of Coleman Saunders
episodes.summary: The Washington Circle pursuit of Coleman Saunders was a crowd chase of a Black man through the streets of Washington, D.C., on the night of August 3, 1910, after he was accused of striking a park watchman, Presley Griffin. According to The Washington Herald, nearly 100 men and boys joined the hunt with cries of "Lynch him!" and broke into the shanty where he hid, but he escaped through a rear window. Police arrested Saunders the next afternoon, and he was later indicted for assault with a dangerous weapon.

episodes.title: Georgetown police clash (1910)
episodes.summary: The Georgetown police clash was a street fight on the night of August 9, 1910, in the Georgetown section of Washington, D.C., between a policeman and a group of about fifteen Black men he had ordered to move on. Four of the men were sentenced in Police Court the next day to thirty to sixty days in jail. White papers outside the capital presented the fight as a "race battle" and a sign that authorities feared "real race riots" in Washington.

episodes.title: Pursuit of Shep Johnson
episodes.summary: The pursuit of Shep Johnson took place on the morning of August 17, 1910, at Thirteenth and C streets southwest in Washington, D.C., when a crowd chased and surrounded a Black man carrying fish in the belief that he had just shot someone. The shot had in fact been fired by William Javins, who had tried to kill himself, and a policeman who saw it cleared Johnson before he was harmed. The Washington Times headlined the incident as a threatened lynching.

episodes.title: Assault on W. L. Taylor
episodes.summary: The assault on W. L. Taylor was a beating of a Washington, D.C., attorney by a group of white men, described as "white ruffians," in the summer of 1910. Taylor survived, and by mid-August he was able to go out again. The attack is known only from short notices of his recovery in two of the city's Black weeklies.

episodes.title: Ash Fork shooting of a fleeing Black man by officers (1910)
episodes.summary: The Ash Fork shooting of a fleeing Black man by officers took place on a Sunday evening in August 1910, probably 21 August, at Ash Fork, Arizona, when officers chased an unnamed "colored man" and fired a number of shots at him. The man, who was said to have used his revolver on a Mexican, escaped into the foothills, and no injury to him was reported. The only known account is a short paragraph in the Williams News.

episodes.title: Killing of Fletcher Reeves
episodes.summary: The killing of Fletcher Reeves was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Patrolman R. L. Leath at a Black dance pavilion in Gadsden, Alabama, at midnight on the night of August 11-12, 1910. Leath was arresting Reeves for selling whiskey, and the only published account, a brief dispatch carrying the officer's version, said Reeves struck him and tried to take his gun. The dispatch ran in white papers in at least three states within a week, and no Black-press coverage was found.

episodes.title: Bay Minette manhunt and arrest of Keyser Brown
episodes.doubt: posse manhunt with stated lynching intent after Marshal Smith's killing (Aug 17); Brown shot before arrest; Perdue beatings near Muscogee are a separate thread (lead)
episodes.summary: The Bay Minette manhunt and arrest of Keyser Brown was an August 1910 pursuit by armed Alabama posses of Black turpentine workers accused of killing Bay Minette's marshal, ending with Brown's capture near Muscogee, Florida, on August 22. Brown was already wounded by gunshots, and Pensacola officers held him for five days because they expected him to be lynched in Baldwin County. The deputy who arrested him also beat two Black men named Perdue near Muscogee and was dismissed and arrested.

episodes.title: Killing of Tom Leverett
episodes.summary: The killing of Tom Leverett was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Chief of Police L. M. Murphy and Officer J. C. Shirley in Anderson, South Carolina, on the afternoon of August 27, 1910. The two officers, who had come to arrest Leverett for "drinking and creating a disturbance," fired through a wooden partition into a closet where he had shut himself with a pistol, and eight bullets struck him. Murphy and Shirley were later tried for the killing, and the judge directed a verdict of not guilty. White South Carolina weeklies carried the officers' account under headlines such as "Negro Desperado Killed."

episodes.title: Police shooting of William Watkins
episodes.summary: The police shooting of William Watkins took place in Lynchburg, Virginia, late on the night of August 12, 1910, when Policeman Kelly shot Watkins, a Black man, as he tried to escape arrest on a charge of snatching a white woman's purse. Watkins was first reported dying, but he survived, was jailed, and was sent on to the grand jury for highway robbery. Only Virginia white papers reported the case, all from the police side.

episodes.title: Manitou streetcar mob threat against William Johnson
episodes.summary: The Manitou streetcar mob threat against William Johnson took place on August 14, 1910, when a crowd of nearly 500 surrounded Johnson, a Black porter of Colorado Springs, at the end of the car line in Manitou, Colorado, after he was accused of insolence to a white woman over a seat. Police removed him to the county jail, and four days later a jury fined him $1 and costs after the evidence failed to show insolence. The Denver Star used the case to attack the white daily press for its eagerness to report a lynching over streetcar manners.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of John Wayne and Charles Clyburn
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of John Wayne and Charles Clyburn took place on the nights of August 28 and 29, 1910, when crowds surrounded the Cabell County jail in Huntington, West Virginia, to take and lynch the two Black prisoners, both held on murder charges. Deputies, police, firemen and militia drove the crowds off under martial law, and neither man was taken. The riot ran on the national wire, led to the indictment of three alleged mob leaders, and drew West Virginia editorials on mob law.

episodes.title: Shooting at Henry Beck's farm, Carroll County, Mississippi
episodes.summary: The shooting at Henry Beck's farm was the killing of five Black men and the mortal wounding of two others by Deputy Sheriff Sid Cauley of Carroll County, Mississippi, in late July or early August 1910. According to the only dispatch, from Elliott, the men attacked the deputy with axes and pitchforks when he came to arrest them, and he shot all seven in about ten seconds. The story spread as a short wire item, drew a mocking editorial in praise of Mississippi marksmanship from the Chicago Inter Ocean, and was cited by the Seattle Republican as an example of wholesale killing of Black people.

episodes.title: Steve Green extradition case
episodes.doubt: the shooting of Green near Jericho was Feb or March 1910; August = interception at Cairo and lynching fears if returned
episodes.summary: The Steve Green extradition case was a 1910 effort by Black Chicagoans to keep Steve Green, a Black farm worker charged with killing a white planter near Jericho, Arkansas, from being returned to Arkansas to be lynched. An Arkansas officer taking Green south was stopped at Cairo, Illinois, by a telegraphed habeas corpus writ, and on September 19 a Chicago judge discharged him. The Black press hailed the outcome as a rescue from lynching.

episodes.title: Coney Island attack on Black bathers (1910)
episodes.summary: The Coney Island attack on Black bathers was an attempted lynching in which a crowd of white bathers at Coney Island, New York, set upon two Black men, Bryant Teal and Frank Davis, in late July 1910 because they had entered the surf alongside white men and women. Davis was dragged into deep water, apparently to drown him, and Teal was chased under a hail of stones, but both escaped. Wire reports carried it in Southern papers as an attempt to lynch, while the Black press reprinted a New York editorial that ridiculed the attackers' claim to a "white man's ocean."

episodes.title: Shooting of Perry McGee
episodes.summary: The shooting of Perry McGee was the wounding of a Black cavalry private, wanted for killing two Black infantrymen, by a constable and an armed villager at Boonville, New York, on August 30, 1910. McGee, reported to have fired on his pursuers first, was shot in the back while in a canal, and physicians at first said he could not live. Wire accounts ran in white papers from New England to Texas, and a later report placed him alive in a Watertown hospital.

episodes.title: Douglas Club shooting
episodes.summary: The Douglas Club shooting was a fight between a party of white men and Black patrons at the Douglas Club, a Black resort at 147 West 28th Street in New York's Tenderloin, late on the night of August 12, 1910. According to the New-York Tribune, the fight began when one of the white visitors threw a whiskey bottle that struck a Black woman singer on the head, and three of the white men were shot before police cleared the club. Associated Press dispatches carried the story across the country as a "race riot," and two Black men connected with the club were held on charges of felonious assault.

episodes.title: New Orleans knife fight over alleged insolence to a patrolman's wife
episodes.summary: The New Orleans knife fight over alleged insolence to a patrolman's wife was a fight in New Orleans, Louisiana, reported on August 31, 1910, between three white men and a group of Black men, after which a Black man lay unconscious and possibly dying. The white men said they had only rebuked the Black men for "insolence" toward the wife of a city patrolman and had been attacked, and the single surviving report gave only their version.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Arthur Neill
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Arthur Neill took place at Vinegar Bend, Washington County, Alabama, on August 22, 1910, when citizens talked of lynching a Black prisoner reported to have confessed to assaulting a white woman, Mrs. J. O. Gibson of Axis. Mobile deputies took him by freight train to the Mobile jail, and he was not harmed. Within weeks, reports said a second confession of his was false and that a grand jury had declined to hold him because he was "crazy" and had confessed though innocent.

episodes.title: Killing of James Ross
episodes.summary: The killing of James Ross was the fatal shooting of a 40-year-old Black man by Biloxi police officer R. M. Randolph on the afternoon of July 31, 1910, in Biloxi, Mississippi. A coroner's jury found the killing justifiable homicide the same day, and the only known report, a special dispatch to The Hattiesburg News, presented it as the end of a drunken rampage.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Cleve Toles and John Calvin
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Cleve Toles and John Calvin took place at Luverne, Alabama, on August 28, 1910, when a crowd reported at more than 300 men gathered to go to Troy and lynch two Black men accused of an attempted assault on a white woman, Clair Fonville. Officials moved the prisoners by automobile from Troy to the Montgomery County jail before the crowd could reach them, and three weeks later both were convicted in the Crenshaw County circuit court and sentenced to twenty years.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Charles Howard
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Charles Howard took place just before daylight on August 28, 1910, when a mob of about 200 men stormed the jail at Frankfort, Kentucky, intending to lynch Howard, a Black man charged with the murder of Edward Rice. The mob was turned away without injury, and the town's jailer and mayor moved Howard to the jail at Lexington. The episode drew a grand jury charge from Judge R. L. Stout, who demanded that the mob's members be brought to justice.

episodes.title: Arcadia, Oklahoma, polling-place confrontation
episodes.summary: The Arcadia, Oklahoma, polling-place confrontation took place on the afternoon of 2 August 1910, when an election inspector at Arcadia drew a revolver and threatened to shoot a group of about 30 Black men lined up at the polls. The crowd dispersed, no one was reported hurt, and the polls were closed until more ballots arrived. The only report found, an Oklahoma City dispatch to the Chickasha Daily Express, presented the incident as a "race riot" narrowly averted.

episodes.title: Marshville freight train shooting
episodes.summary: The Marshville freight train shooting took place in Marshville, North Carolina, on Thursday, 28 July 1910, when Policeman Ashcraft chased and fired on two Black men who had jumped from a freight train. One of the men was thought to be the killer of a constable, but the man caught proved to be only a train rider, and the other escaped.

episodes.title: Attempted lynchings of Tom Hayes
episodes.summary: The attempted lynchings of Tom Hayes were two efforts by crowds in Covington County, Alabama, in the summer of 1910 to seize and kill Hayes, a Black man accused of murdering R. D. Sowell, a white night watchman at a lumber yard near Andalusia. On July 31 a crowd of mill workers pursued the officers' automobile carrying Hayes to the railroad station at Gantt, and on the night of August 24 a mob reported at 250 men planned to storm the Andalusia jail. Hayes escaped both times, by automobile and train on the first occasion and under a militia guard on the second, and was held in the Montgomery County jail.

episodes.title: Manhunt for Will Jones
episodes.doubt: at Bostick's Mill, six miles SE of Tunica; lynching feared on capture
episodes.summary: The manhunt for Will Jones was a posse pursuit with bloodhounds near Tunica, Mississippi, in late August 1910, after Jones, a Black farm employee, was accused of trying to pull a nine-year-old white girl through her bedroom window. Dispatches said he had been located and that a lynching was feared if he was caught, but no report of his capture or fate was found.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Black residents from Davis, Oklahoma
episodes.summary: The expulsion of Black residents from Davis, Oklahoma, took place in August 1910, when white townsmen threatened the town's Black population after a Black man struck a white man with a brickbat. A local report said about 25 of some 75 Black residents fled, most to Ardmore, while an Oklahoma City dispatch said every Black resident was driven out.

episodes.title: Lynching of Laura Porter
episodes.summary: The lynching of Laura Porter was the seizure of a Black woman from the city jail of Monroe, Louisiana, in late July 1910 by unidentified men, who were believed to have drowned her in the Ouachita River. No trace of her was reported found, and a Louisiana weekly described the affair as "what appears to have been a lynching." A South Carolina paper ran the news under the headline "Shame on Louisiana."

episodes.title: Lynching of Elmo Curl
episodes.doubt: date not given; hanged before Aug 3
episodes.summary: The lynching of Elmo Curl was the hanging of Curl by a gathering of local men at Mastodon, Mississippi, in the summer of 1910. The Washington Herald described Curl as "a negro," and no paper reported what he was accused of. The case became known outside the South through a letter insisting that the hanging had been "a most orderly affair" carried out by the county's "best people," which northern and western papers reprinted and ridiculed in August and September 1910.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Jesse James (Leola, Arkansas)
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Jesse James took place in August 1910 near Leola, Grant County, Arkansas, when a mob gathered to capture James, a Black man accused of attempting to assault a fourteen-year-old girl. City Marshal Charles Stephens arrested him and took him by way of Pine Bluff to the county jail at Sheridan, and the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic reported that he would otherwise have been lynched.

episodes.title: Killing of Remus White
episodes.summary: The killing of Remus White was the shooting of a Black man accused of taking part in the murder of Jesse Baldwin by a deputy sheriff who was arresting him in Conecuh County, Alabama, in July 1910. His death surfaced in the press only weeks later, as an aside in reports on the capture of another suspect and on a mob's attempt on the Evergreen jail. The reports differ on his first name, the deputy's name and the timing.

episodes.title: Raggio dance hall shooting
episodes.summary: The Raggio dance hall shooting was a gun battle at a dance at Raggio, twelve miles east of Marianna in Lee County, Arkansas, at about 1 a.m. on Sunday, August 28, 1910, in which two Black men, Mack Harvey and Henry Cox, were killed and three others wounded. It began when a white man, John Russell, returned to the dance with two men the county sheriff called deputy constables to arrest Harvey, and Russell himself was fatally shot. Wire reports of a battle of more than fifty shots between "negroes and whites" ran in papers from Arkansas to Connecticut.

episodes.title: Killing of Orville Wright in Kansas City
episodes.summary: The killing of Orville Wright was the fatal shooting of a Black boy by William T. Cox, a Kansas City police patrolman, on a Wednesday afternoon in August 1910. Wright died in the city's old general hospital, and within days Cox was dismissed from the force and charged with first-degree murder.

episodes.title: Marion lynching threat (1910)
episodes.summary: The Marion lynching threat was a lynching scare in Marion, Perry County, Alabama, on Sunday, August 7, 1910, after night watchman Calhoun Watters was shot and Black men were jailed as suspects. Crowds of country citizens gathered and a lynching at one time seemed likely, but no attack on the jail took place. By the end of the month the men were seeking release on bond, with the evidence against them described as all circumstantial.

episodes.title: Police shooting of Charles Smith in Philadelphia
episodes.summary: The police shooting of Charles Smith took place early on August 7, 1910, at Ninth and Clinton streets in Philadelphia, when Policeman Markey fired on Smith, a Black man, as he ran from an alleged street robbery. Hit by two bullets, Smith was taken to the Pennsylvania Hospital in serious condition and held there under police guard.

episodes.title: Cherokee shooting of a man mistaken for Bob Hibble
episodes.summary: The Cherokee shooting of a man mistaken for Bob Hibble took place on the morning of August 27, 1910, near Cherokee, eighteen miles west of Tuscumbia, when a Black man hunted as Bob Hibble, a fugitive wanted for murder in Attalla County, Mississippi, was captured in a deserted schoolhouse and shot by officers before he surrendered. Officers who came from Attalla County two days later declared the prisoner to be the wrong man. Alabama papers followed the case for its leap from a fast train, the misidentification, and a Black woman's damage suit against the Southern Railway.

episodes.title: Third Street police shooting, Richmond (1910)
episodes.summary: The Third Street police shooting was an incident in Richmond, Virginia, in August 1910 in which a police officer fired at a Black man he had followed into the yards between Broad and Grace streets. The man was not hurt, and the officer, after checking his explanation, found that he had told the truth. The Richmond Planet reported it under the headline "A Colored Man Has Narrow Escape."

episodes.title: Death of Fred Spencer near Mulga
episodes.doubt: body 'believed' Spencer's; lynching only 'possible'; posse search was April
episodes.summary: The death of Fred Spencer near Mulga, Alabama, came to light in early August 1910, when the body of a Black man believed to be Spencer was found there. Spencer had been sought since April as the accused killer of Capt. B. H. Young, and a Birmingham paper wrote that it was "possible that he was lynched" by men who had hunted him.

episodes.title: Clubbing of Lem Heard at Heflin depot
episodes.summary: The clubbing of Lem Heard at Heflin depot took place on the night of Sunday, July 31, 1910, when deputies used clubs on a crowd of Black people leaving a district conference at Heflin, Alabama, and knocked Heard, a Black resident of the town, senseless. The only report found, a special dispatch to the Montgomery Advertiser, presented the episode as a near "race riot" that extra police had prevented.

episodes.title: Killing of Edwin Nicholson
episodes.summary: The killing of Edwin Nicholson took place on August 15, 1910, on the Hillsboro road in West Raleigh, North Carolina, when a guard shot Nicholson, a Black county convict, as he ran from a Wake county road force. The guard, R. M. Saunders, fired on the foreman's order, and the coroner decided no inquest was needed. A wire version circulated beyond the state, built around Nicholson's reported remark that he would rather be dead than alive.

episodes.title: Police killing of Daniels in Shreveport
episodes.summary: The police killing of Daniels took place on August 18, 1910, when Officer Hebert Waites shot dead a Black man named Daniels after a call to Howell Street, apparently in Shreveport, Louisiana. According to the police account, the only one published, Daniels struck at the officer with a hatchet while being taken to the station, and an inquest was set for that evening.

episodes.title: Slocum massacre
episodes.doubt: grand jury: 8 killed (7 Anderson Co., Will Burley in Houston Co.); estimates 8-40; only Hayes, Holly and Burley named in the coverage seen, other names from B-T; Burley's B-T row bt:4739 also belongs here (folded g136)
episodes.summary: The Slocum massacre was the killing of Black residents by armed white men around Slocum and Denson Springs, south of Palestine in Anderson County, Texas, beginning on the night of July 29, 1910. Sheriff Black estimated fifteen to twenty dead, "all of them probably unarmed," while the grand jury later found eight Black men killed and no white person hurt. Seven white men were indicted for murder, and Black papers called it the "Palestine Massacre."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching at Evergreen, Alabama (1910)
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching at Evergreen, Alabama, was a siege of the Conecuh County jail by about 100 armed men early on Sunday, August 7, 1910, aimed at Black prisoners held in the killing of an aged farmer, Jesse Baldwin. Company K of the Alabama National Guard refused the mob's demands for the jail keys, and the crowd dispersed without anyone being hurt. The two men charged with the murder, Albert Johnson and John Manuel, were moved to Mobile that afternoon, and wire stories carried the episode nationally as a lynching prevented by troops.

episodes.title: Killing of William Brown
episodes.summary: The killing of William Brown took place in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, early on July 31, 1910, when Police Officer Herman Weins shot dead Brown, a Black packing-house worker accused of shooting two officers hours before. During the search, a crowd of about a thousand men demanded that he be lynched, and part of it stoned a house occupied by Black residents. The story ran as far as Kentucky and Ohio, and two South Dakota editors wrote that the state had narrowly escaped a lynching.

episodes.title: Arrest and beating of E. C. and John Perdue
episodes.summary: The arrest and beating of E. C. and John Perdue took place near Muscogee, Escambia County, Florida, on August 22, 1910, when Deputy Sheriff S. T. Andrews arrested the two Black men on a charge of attempted assault on a white woman and clubbed one with his pistol. Sheriff Van Pelt later said the woman had told Andrews the men were not her assailants; he dismissed the deputy, released the men, and arrested Andrews on a warrant sworn out by their father. A mob reportedly formed to take the men from jail, and the Pensacola press treated Andrews's conduct as incitement.
